column1: What is the fundamental structural flaw in Discretionary Access Control (DAC) that SELinux is designed to solve?
column2: Transitivity of privilege: if a privileged process (e.g., root daemon) is compromised, the attacker inherits all of that identity's privileges system-wide, since DAC trusts user identity rather than enforcing fine-grained, process-level policy.

column1: In SELinux's Type Enforcement model, what determines a subject's or object's security-relevant properties?
column2: Labels (security contexts), not Unix identity. A process carries a context like system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 rather than being judged simply as 'root' or 'www-data'.

column1: What is the fundamental default-access invariant of SELinux policy?
column2: All access is denied by default unless an explicit 'allow' rule grants it — there is no implicit permission inherited from group membership or process privilege.

column1: What two orthogonal components did the Flask architecture define to separate policy evaluation from enforcement?
column2: A security server that evaluates policy and renders decisions, and an object manager embedded in the kernel that caches and enforces those decisions.

column1: What kernel framework gives SELinux its integration point into Linux, and how does it work?
column2: Linux Security Modules (LSM), merged in kernel 2.6, which places hook functions at security-relevant operations (open, mmap, connect, execve, mprotect, etc.) that call into the active security module before the kernel's own capability checks complete.

column1: What is the enforcement ordering invariant between DAC and SELinux (MAC) checks in the kernel?
column2: DAC checks always execute first; only if they pass does control flow into SELinux's MAC authorization logic. SELinux supplements DAC, it never replaces it.

column1: What are the three principal runtime components of SELinux's enforcement architecture?
column2: Object managers (request authorization decisions throughout the kernel), the security server (evaluates policy and renders verdicts), and the Access Vector Cache / AVC (memoizes recent decisions to avoid repeated policy evaluation).

column1: What does an Access Vector Cache (AVC) entry map, and what happens when the policy database changes?
column2: An AVC entry maps a (source context, target context, object class) tuple to a permission bitmap. It is write-through: policy modifications immediately invalidate affected entries, forcing recomputation on the next access.

column1: What are the three phases of the SELinux policy lifecycle?
column2: 1) Writing human-readable policy source in a domain-specific language, 2) Compiling it via checkmodule and semodule_package into a binary policy module, 3) Enforcing it entirely in kernel space via the security server and AVC.

column1: What three tools form the SELinux policy compilation/loading toolchain, and what does each do?
column2: checkmodule (syntax validation and module compilation), semodule_package (packages the compiled module), and semodule (loads/integrates the module into the active kernel policy store).

column1: What monotonicity guarantee does the SELinux security server provide regarding denials?
column2: Once a policy decision denies access, no cache manipulation or timing variation can bypass that denial without an explicit policy change — every decision also produces an auditable trail.

column1: Why can't even root bypass SELinux MAC restrictions on a compromised process (e.g., exploited httpd_t)?
column2: Because policy is mandatory and compiled/loaded before runtime by an administrator; a compromised process is confined to the permissions explicitly granted to its labeled domain (e.g., httpd_t), regardless of the Unix UID it runs as, so it cannot open /etc/shadow or load kernel modules unless policy explicitly allows it.
